design_detail: American Heart Association scientific statement (Circulation, 2020; online-first version read, pages e1–e22) by a nine-member writing group on behalf of the AHA Clinical Pharmacology Committee and Heart Failure and Transplantation Committee of the Council on Clinical Cardiology and five other AHA councils; approved by the AHA Science Advisory and Coordinating Committee (18 May 2020) and Executive Committee (22 June 2020) and peer-reviewed through the AHA Office of Science Operations by four named reviewers. It covers definitions and products, pharmacology (Table 1), a dosing section for clinicians, claimed medical benefits sorted into undefined evidence categories (Table 2), acute and cardiovascular effects with a table of 25 “seminal” studies (Table 3), smoking, vaping and impurities, chronic effects, use disorder, drug interactions (Table 4), special populations (young adults, pregnancy, older adults, transplantation, heart disease, cardiac risk factors), patient advice and policy (Table 5). No search strategy, databases, dates, inclusion criteria, appraisal method or grading rules are stated, and nothing is pooled. Filed as evidence-report with the editors' evidence-report checklist, not AMSTAR 2, because it states no systematic search for its conclusions (METHODS §5.3); it is a professional-society statement rather than a report of a public body.
can_establish: What an AHA writing group concluded in mid-2020 about cannabis and cardiovascular health, which studies it chose to tabulate and what it reports they found (as relayed), which weaknesses of that literature it names, and what it recommends to clinicians, the public and policymakers.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis causes any cardiovascular outcome, or how large any effect is: the statement states no search, selection rule, appraisal method or grading rules, pools nothing, and relays estimates (most without intervals or adjustment sets, several misreported) from mainly administrative hospital databases, surveys, case reports and pharmacovigilance; its statements on psychosis, cognition, dependence, pregnancy and driving are second-hand from other reviews, single studies or uncited.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (evidence report without a stated search). Sources are 100 references chosen by the writing group: agency and other web pages (Health Canada, SAMHSA/NSDUH, FDA, CDC, NIDA, US Surgeon General, a map provider, a CNN article), the 2017 National Academies report, narrative reviews (notably DeFilippis et al., 2020, JACC, ref 20), one meeting abstract (ref 18), and 25 studies in Table 3 (refs 19 and 26–49).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated. Table 3 is titled “Seminal Studies on the Impact of Cannabis on Cardiovascular Health” without a selection rule.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the writing group's and unexplained. Table 3 is weighted toward US administrative inpatient data: 7 of 25 rows are National Inpatient Sample analyses (refs 27, 33–36, 41, 45), five of them including the years 2010–2014 and four by the same first author, so they are not independent; 4 rows come from one cohort (CARDIA, refs 29, 30, 46, 48) and 2 from one study (Determinants of Myocardial Infarction Onset Study, refs 37, 43); 2 rows are systematic reviews of case reports and studies. A 2018 systematic review of cannabis and cardiovascular risk factors and outcomes on this project's list (Ravi et al., Annals of Internal Medicine) is not cited, and no genetically informed study is cited for any outcome. One writing-group member co-authored three of the four CARDIA papers tabulated (refs 29, 30, 46).

exposure.measurement: Varies across the cited sources and is rarely stated: a recorded history of cannabis use or cannabis-related diagnosis or billing codes in inpatient and health-record databases (National Inpatient Sample; Explorys, where the group is labelled “cannabis abuse”); a cannabis-use-disorder codiagnosis (ref 45); past-year use in a population survey, and use weekly or more often (ref 38), or use on more than 10 days a month (ref 68); cumulative lifetime and recent use (CARDIA, units not given); “long-term heavy” use (ref 42, undefined); use within 1 or 24 hours before MI onset (ref 43); ED chart attribution by route (ref 19); daily use and high-potency cannabis, THC 10% or more (EU-GEI, ref 67). The statement names lack of exposure determination, recall bias and minimal exposure without dose or product standardisation as general weaknesses (p. e9).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesised. No cardiovascular estimate is given by dose or potency; frequency appears only in the stroke studies (weekly or more; more than 10 days a month) and route only in the ED study (edible vs inhaled) and in statements on smoke (carbon monoxide, tar). The statement's DOSING section for clinicians (pp. e4, e6, e8) and the dose-adjustment cells of Table 4 were read but are not extracted, by project rule.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco co-use is named as a major confounder inadequately handled in data collection and adjustment (p. e10). Handling in the cited studies, as relayed: CARDIA calcification analysed separately by tobacco history (ref 29); stroke analyses adjusted for tobacco (ref 38) or stratified by cigarette and e-cigarette co-use (ref 68); one inpatient analysis restricted to cannabis without other substance use (ref 33); one MI registry reported as cocaine and marijuana use together (ref 32). For the rest, adjustment for other drugs is not stated.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (outcomes are events, diagnoses or survey reports). Timing of use relative to the event appears only in the triggering study (within 60 minutes or 24 hours before MI onset) and in a review of case reports (AMI within 5 hours of last use).

comparison.controls: Within the cited studies: other patients in the same database without recorded cannabis use, people who did not report use in surveys, never use (EU-GEI), the same person's control periods (case-crossover, ref 43), propensity-matched patients (heart failure abstract, Table 2); no comparison group in case reports, pharmacovigilance or the arrhythmia analysis of ref 36 as relayed.
comparison.matching: Only the heart failure abstract (propensity matching) and the case-crossover design (self-matching) are described; for most Table 3 rows neither matching nor adjustment is stated.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The statement names access to health care, other adverse health behaviours and tobacco as likely confounders (p. e9) and says the EU-GEI study did not account for genetic and environmental factors (p. e14). Socio-economic position, diet, physical activity, stimulant use and baseline cardiovascular risk are not discussed study by study; administrative data carry no pre-use measures.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Generally not addressed: comparison groups in inpatient databases are other hospitalised patients, whose drug use is not described; only ref 33 excludes other substance use.

outcomes.instruments: Cited outcomes: incident cardiovascular disease, coronary heart disease, stroke or TIA and cardiac mortality (CARDIA); abdominal aortic and coronary artery calcium scores (CARDIA); blood pressure, prediabetes and diabetes (NHANES, CARDIA); AMI, heart failure, arrhythmia, stroke and venous thromboembolism as hospital diagnoses (National Inpatient Sample, Explorys, state hospital records); in-hospital mortality, a composite in-hospital outcome, length of stay and costs; long-term mortality (National Death Index); timing of MI onset (case-crossover interview); ED chart diagnoses (ref 19); pharmacovigilance reports (ref 39); cardiac death rates in vital statistics (ref 26); exercise time to angina and haemodynamics (1970s laboratory studies, refs 88, 89).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed: validation of diagnosis codes or of self-reported cannabis use in administrative data is not mentioned.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is any reported association between cannabis use and a cardiovascular event, diagnosis or risk factor in a cited study; none is graded. Claimed benefits are sorted in Table 2 into “Known (conclusive or substantial evidence)”, “Possible (moderate evidence)” and “Inconclusive evidence (no RCTs)”, categories that are not defined.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled or new estimates. Estimates relayed from cited studies (exposure, comparator and adjustment as printed; most rows give neither interval nor adjustment set). Cardiovascular events: Chami and Kim (ref 31), 3-year AMI incidence 1.37% vs 0.54%, RR 2.53 (95% CI 2.45–2.61); Desai et al. 2017 (ref 34), AMI adjusted OR 1.079 (1.065–1.093); Desai et al. 2019 (ref 33), AMI admissions in young adults 0.23% vs 0.14%; Kalla et al. (ref 41), heart failure OR 1.1 and stroke OR 1.24; Mittleman et al. (ref 43), MI onset 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after use (no interval); Hemachandra et al. (ref 38), stroke or TIA IRR 3.3 (1.8–6.3) before and 2.3 (1.1–4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco, 4.7 (2.1–10.7) for weekly or more frequent use; Parekh et al. (ref 68), stroke adjusted OR 1.82 (1.08–3.10), 2.45 (1.31–4.60) for use on more than 10 days a month, 3.12 (1.40–6.97) for frequent use with combustible-cigarette use and 2.63 (1.07–6.46) for frequent use with e-cigarette use, against people who did not use cannabis; Reis et al. (ref 46, CARDIA), no association (no estimate printed); Adegbala et al. (ref 27), atrial fibrillation 19% vs 21% in heart failure. Mortality: Frost et al. (ref 37), 29% higher after MI, 95% CI 0.81–2.05, P = 0.28; DeFilippis et al. 2018 (ref 32), adjusted HR 1.99 all-cause and 2.22 cardiovascular among people who used cocaine and marijuana; Johnson-Sasso et al. (ref 40), mortality OR 0.79 (short-term outcomes, by the reference title); heart failure abstract (Table 2), in-hospital death OR 0.197 (0.046–0.833). Risk factors: Alshaarawy et al. (ref 28), systolic pressure β 1.6 (0.6–2.7). Mental health and pregnancy (second-hand): EU-GEI daily use adjusted OR 3.2 (2.2–4.1) and daily high-potency use printed as adjusted OR 3.2 (3.0–16.1); Gobbi et al. depression OR 1.37 (1.16–1.62), suicidal ideation 1.5 (1.11–2.03), suicide attempt 3.46 (1.53–7.84); Crume et al. low birth weight OR 1.5 (1.1–2.1); Gunn et al. anaemia OR 1.36 (1.10–1.69), low birth weight OR 1.77 (1.04–3.01), birth weight mean difference 109.42 g (38.72–180.12). Editors' calculation (geometric midpoints of the printed intervals): about 7.0 for 3.0–16.1 and about 3.0 for 2.2–4.1, so neither EU-GEI point estimate of 3.2 sits at the centre of its interval; the other ratio estimates with intervals listed here are centred to rounding.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at report level. Adjustment sets are named only for Hemachandra et al. (covariates related to stroke, including tobacco smoking) and Crume et al. (maternal age, race or ethnicity, education, tobacco); elsewhere estimates are labelled adjusted or multivariable without the covariates, or are crude.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Null and protective findings are relayed as well as harmful ones (CARDIA; Frost et al.; Adegbala et al.; Johnson-Sasso et al.; lower venous thromboembolism in ref 33; the heart failure abstract), but intervals are printed in only 5 of the 25 Table 3 rows, three rows give no figures in the results column (Auer, Bancks, Lorenz) and two give no effect estimate (Reis, Rodondi). A systematic review on the same question on this project's list that predates the statement (Ravi et al., 2018) is not cited.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The statement has no new data. Its tabulated evidence (25 studies, Table 3) is mostly US administrative hospital databases, surveys, case reports and pharmacovigilance, with few prospective cohorts. In CARDIA (5113 young adults followed for more than 25 years) cumulative and recent use were not associated with incident cardiovascular disease; hospital-database studies report more AMI, stroke and arrhythmia among people with recorded cannabis use, with crude or unstated adjustment; a case-crossover study reports a transient 4.8-fold rise in MI onset in the hour after use, resting on 9 people exposed in that hour; two surveys report higher stroke rates, concentrated in frequent use (IRR 2.3 for past-year use after adjustment including tobacco and 4.7 for weekly or more, adjustment not stated; adjusted OR 2.45 for use on more than 10 days a month); outcomes after MI are mixed (lower in-hospital mortality in two database studies, a non-significant 29% higher long-term mortality, and hazard ratios near 2 for people who used cocaine and marijuana). The authors' own summary is that the cardiovascular evidence is inconclusive and, for people with cardiac risk factors, insufficient.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract lists cardiovascular diseases among the “concerning health implications” of cannabis (p. e1), a framing stronger than the body's “still inconclusive” (p. e10) and “insufficient” (p. e17). Several sentences go beyond the studies cited for them: AMI hospitalisations and ED visits are said to have risen where cannabis is legal, citing a vital-statistics study of cardiac deaths and an unrelated CARDIA analysis (p. e10); worse all-cause and cardiovascular mortality is attributed to cannabis from hazard ratios Table 3 gives for people who used cocaine and marijuana (pp. e11, e17); mechanisms (sympathetic stimulation, raised myocardial oxygen demand and supine blood pressure, platelet activation, endothelial dysfunction, lower myocardial oxygen supply) are stated without hedging on the strength of reviews and two 1970s laboratory studies (pp. e9, e17); clinical consequences of carbon monoxide poisoning (ref 24) are carried over to cannabis smoke (p. e9); regular adolescent use “may lead to” brain structural changes on observational imaging (p. e14). Recommendations are made without stated grading: cannabis vaping should be avoided although the vitamin E acetate evidence is called limited (p. e13); cannabis arteritis should be considered in adults under 50 with peripheral vascular disease although the estimate is called confounded (p. e10); negative health implications should be emphasised in policy (p. e19). Against this, the body states its uncertainty plainly, names selection bias and tobacco confounding, and relays null and protective findings.

timeline.event: Aronow and Cassidy: in people with stable angina, one cannabis cigarette shortened exercise time to angina by 48% against placebo (as cited by the statement, ref 88; sample size not given).
Wu, Tashkin and colleagues compare cannabis and tobacco smoke; the statement relays a 5-fold rise in carboxyhaemoglobin and 3-fold more tar (ref 23, not read).

Mittleman et al., case-crossover study of 3882 people with AMI: MI onset 4.8 times baseline in the hour after cannabis use, 9 people exposed in that hour (as cited, ref 43; on this project's Tier B list).
Rodondi et al. (CARDIA): associations of cannabis use with systolic pressure and triglycerides disappear after multivariable adjustment (as cited, ref 48).
Frost et al.: long-term mortality after MI 29% higher in people who used cannabis, not significant (95% CI 0.81–2.05); same study as Mittleman 2001 (as cited, ref 37).
Jouanjus et al.: French addictovigilance, cardiovascular share of cannabis-related reports up from 1.1% to 3.6% over 2006–2010 (as cited, ref 39; Tier B).

Hemachandra et al. (PATH Through Life): stroke or TIA with past-year use, IRR 3.3 before and 2.3 after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco, the excess confined to weekly or more frequent use (as cited, ref 38).

National Academies report, cited by the statement (ref 12) for its respiratory, withdrawal, psychosis, cognition and pregnancy statements; its own smoke comparison in 15 volunteers gives about four times the carbon monoxide and three to five times the tar of a cigarette (card sc_nasem_2017).

Reis et al. (CARDIA, 5113 adults, more than 25 years): cumulative lifetime and recent use not associated with incident cardiovascular disease, stroke or TIA, coronary disease or cardiac mortality (as cited, ref 46; the text cites it as ref 29 by error).
Auer et al. (CARDIA): higher aortic and coronary calcium with marijuana exposure only in people who had ever smoked tobacco, a check on tobacco confounding (as cited, ref 29).

US National Inpatient Sample analyses published 2017–2019 (Desai et al., four papers; Kalla et al.; Patel et al.; Adegbala et al.): more AMI, arrhythmia and stroke diagnoses among hospitalised people with recorded cannabis use; the statement warns of selection bias in hospital-only samples. Overlapping years of one database, not independent replications.
Chami and Kim: 3-year AMI incidence 1.37% vs 0.54%, RR 2.53, in an aggregated health-record database, adjustment not stated (as cited, ref 31).
Monte et al.: edible against inhaled cannabis in ED visits at one Colorado hospital (ref 19); appraised from its full text in this library.

Di Forti et al. (EU-GEI): daily and high-potency use and psychotic disorder; relayed with misprinted figures and the caveat that genetic and environmental factors were not accounted for (ref 67; Tier A on this project's list).
Gobbi et al.: meta-analysis of adolescent cannabis use and later depression and suicidality (ref 66; Tier A).
Parekh et al. (BRFSS): stroke in adults aged 18–44, adjusted OR 1.82, and 2.45 with use on more than 10 days a month (as cited, ref 68).
DeFilippis et al., JACC review of marijuana use in people with cardiovascular disease (ref 20): the statement's main source for mechanisms, confounding caveats and drug interactions.
This statement (approved June 2020): cardiovascular evidence judged inconclusive; no well-documented cardiovascular benefits.

replication.where_it_stands: A mid-2020 professional-society summary, not a test. Within its own pages the cardiovascular evidence divides by design: the long CARDIA cohort found no association with incident cardiovascular disease, while hospital-database, case-crossover, survey and case-report studies report associations with AMI, stroke and arrhythmia; the statement calls the evidence inconclusive. It discusses confounding by tobacco (CARDIA calcification only in people who had smoked tobacco; arteritis estimates confounded by 97% tobacco co-use), selection bias in hospital-only samples and the relevance of older studies given rising THC content, but cites no genetically informed or sibling designs for any outcome; its within-person evidence is the case-crossover study, and its quasi-experimental evidence is limited to vital-statistics and Colorado trends around legalisation, which it does not appraise. For psychosis it relays EU-GEI with a confounding caveat; for cognition and dependence it gives second-hand or uncited summaries. Primary studies to appraise directly from this project's lists: Mittleman et al. (2001), Jouanjus et al. (2014) and Ravi et al. (2018, not cited by the statement) on Tier B; Jeffers et al. (2024, published later) on Tier C; Di Forti et al. (2019), Gobbi et al. (2019) and Gunn et al. (2016) on Tier A. The CARDIA papers of Reis et al. (2017) and Auer et al. (2018) are not yet on the lists.

funding.affiliations_note: Writing group: University of Colorado Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences (Page, chair), University of Colorado School of Medicine (Allen, vice chair), High Point University (Carriker), Huntington Medical Research Institutes Cardiovascular Research Institute (Kloner), Montreal Heart Institute Research Center, Université de Montréal (Martel), Emory University School of Medicine (Morris), Vanderbilt University School of Nursing (Piano), Kaiser Permanente Northern California (Rana), Medical College of Wisconsin (Saucedo). Rana is a co-author of three CARDIA papers in Table 3 (refs 29, 30, 46) and Kloner of a cited review of cardiovascular effects (ref 22, a source of Figure 5). The policy section states an AHA commitment to limiting the smoking and vaping of any products and to banning cannabis use for youth (p. e19). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the cardiovascular question: large prospective cohorts, or a pooled analysis of existing ones, with repeated, validated measures of cannabis frequency, route and potency and of tobacco use, analysed separately in people who have never smoked tobacco, with adjudicated MI, stroke, arrhythmia and cardiovascular death and absolute risks by age and baseline risk; case-crossover studies with objectively timed exposure for acute triggering; and genetically informed or sibling designs to separate cannabis from shared risk factors. A systematic review with a stated search and risk-of-bias appraisal, which this statement is not, would then be needed to summarise them.

domains.note: No search strategy, databases, dates, terms or inclusion criteria; the authors call the document a critical review (p. e1) and Table 3 “seminal studies” without saying how they were chosen. Sources include web pages and a news article, a meeting abstract (ref 18) and narrative reviews; a 2018 systematic review on the same question on this project's list is not cited.

No appraisal tool or study-by-study judgment. General weaknesses are named (short-term observational designs, poor exposure measurement, recall bias, low-risk cohorts, confounding by health-care access and tobacco, selection bias in hospital-only samples; pp. e9–e10) and the heart failure abstract is labelled not peer reviewed, but Table 3 relays estimates without design labels, intervals or adjustment sets for most rows and contains entries that cannot be right as printed (reporting issues), which suggests the entries were not checked against what each design can show.
No grading system, classes of recommendation or levels of evidence. Table 2 uses undefined categories (known, possible, inconclusive) and applies them inconsistently; harms are not graded at all.

No funding statement. All writing-group members and reviewers declare no relationships. A writing-group member co-authored three of the tabulated CARDIA papers and another a cited review; the conclusion states an organisational commitment to limiting smoking and vaping of any product (p. e19), which frames several recommendations.

Peer review through the AHA Office of Science Operations, four named reviewers with disclosures, approval by two AHA committees with dates (pp. e19–e20). Reviewer comments are not published, and the citation and table errors listed on this card were not caught.

The body's summary judgments stay within the evidence it describes (inconclusive, p. e10; insufficient, p. e17; no well-documented cardiovascular benefits, p. e8). The abstract's framing, mechanistic statements made as facts, the carry-over from carbon monoxide poisoning, a causal verb for adolescent imaging, misattributed mortality and AMI-trend sentences, and ungraded recommendations go further (interpretation gap).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Filed as design evidence-report with the editors' evidence-report checklist, as the brief directs, and not with AMSTAR 2, because the statement states no systematic search for its conclusions (METHODS §5.3). It is a professional-society statement, externally reviewed and approved by the AHA, but with no stated search, selection rule, appraisal method or grading rules, so the checklist gives no reason to weight it above a narrative review; the overall judgment is high, as the worst domains require. It may be cited for the AHA's own judgments, attributed to the AHA (cardiovascular evidence inconclusive; no well-documented cardiovascular benefits; evidence insufficient for people with cardiac risk factors; its recommendations), for the weaknesses of the literature it names, and as a pointer to primary studies. Every figure on this card is second-hand and should be cited from the primary study named with it, after that study has been read; the statement must not be cited for pharmacology, for dependence figures (uncited), for the EU-GEI high-potency estimate (misprinted), or for the AMI-trend and mortality sentences that its own table does not support.

key_findings.finding: Method as stated: the writing group describes the document as a critical review of medicinal and recreational cannabis from clinical, policy and public-health perspectives, focused on cardiovascular health. No search strategy, databases, dates, inclusion criteria, appraisal method or grading system is described anywhere. It was approved by the AHA Science Advisory and Coordinating Committee on 18 May 2020 and the AHA Executive Committee on 22 June 2020, and peer-reviewed through the AHA Office of Science Operations by four named reviewers.

key_findings.finding: The AHA's overall cardiovascular judgment: evidence on cannabis use and adverse cardiovascular outcomes is “still inconclusive”, with an urgent need for carefully designed prospective short- and long-term studies and, ideally, controlled trials of different forms and routes, which the authors say remain hard to do for recreational drugs.

key_findings.finding: No well-documented cardiovascular benefits of cannabis (summary of Table 2, refs 5, 12, 13, 17, 18); the abstract says cannabis may have therapeutic benefits but few are cardiovascular. For people with cardiac risk factors the statement judges the present evidence for a link between cannabis use and health outcomes insufficient, citing limited longitudinal data and recall bias in cross-sectional studies.

key_findings.finding: Weaknesses of the cardiovascular literature as the statement names them (citing the DeFilippis et al. 2020 review, ref 20, and a NIDA web page, ref 25): most data are short-term, observational and retrospective; exposure is poorly determined and open to recall bias; exposure is minimal, with no dose or product standardisation; cohorts are typically low-risk; epidemiological studies may be confounded by access to health care and other behaviours such as tobacco use; older studies may not reflect current, higher THC concentrations; few data come from rigorous prospective cohorts. Studies restricted to hospitalised patients analyse only a fraction of the people with an outcome and carry a high probability of selection bias, so cannabis as a cause of hospitalisation is uncertain; tobacco and other drug co-use is inadequately handled in data collection and adjustment.

key_findings.finding: Table 3 (“Seminal Studies”) lists 25 studies (refs 19 and 26–49) without a selection rule or quality rating: 7 National Inpatient Sample analyses (refs 27, 33–36, 41, 45), other hospital or health-record data (refs 31, 32, 40, 49), two surveys (NHANES, ref 28; PATH Through Life, ref 38), 4 papers from CARDIA (refs 29, 30, 46, 48), an HIV cohort (ref 42), two papers from the Determinants of Myocardial Infarction Onset Study (refs 37, 43), a pharmacovigilance series (ref 39), vital statistics around medical cannabis laws (ref 26), one ED chart review (ref 19) and two systematic reviews of case reports and studies (refs 44, 47). Confidence intervals are printed in 5 rows; three rows give no figures in the results column (Auer, Bancks, Lorenz).

key_findings.finding: CARDIA, incident disease (Reis et al., 2017, ref 46): 5113 adults aged 18–30 at the 1985–1986 baseline, followed for more than 25 years; 84% reported a history of cannabis use. Cumulative lifetime and recent use (units not given) showed no association with incident cardiovascular disease, stroke or TIA, coronary heart disease or cardiac mortality. No estimates, intervals or adjustment set are printed.

key_findings.note: The text cites this finding to ref 29 (Auer et al., 2018) and omits stroke or TIA; Table 3 and the reference list give it to ref 46 (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Other CARDIA papers as relayed: Auer et al., 2018 (ref 29; 3498 participants): among people who had ever smoked tobacco, marijuana exposure was associated with higher abdominal aortic and coronary artery calcium scores, and among people who had never smoked tobacco it was not (no numbers). Bancks et al., 2015 (ref 30; more than 3000): cannabis use in young adulthood associated with higher risk of prediabetes but not diabetes by middle adulthood (no numbers). Rodondi et al., 2006 (ref 48; 3617 with 15 years of data): 38% had ever used cannabis; use was associated with male sex, tobacco and other illicit drug use, higher caloric and alcohol intake, systolic blood pressure (113–117 mm Hg) and triglycerides, but not with BMI, lipids or glucose; after multivariable adjustment it was not associated with systolic pressure or triglycerides.

key_findings.note: The text cites the calcification finding to ref 46 instead of ref 29 (reporting issue). Ever-use is 84% in one CARDIA row and 38% in another, with no definitions.

key_findings.finding: Triggering (Mittleman et al., 2001, ref 43; Determinants of Myocardial Infarction Onset Study, case-crossover, 3882 people with AMI): risk of MI onset 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after cannabis use (no interval printed). 3% had smoked cannabis in the prior year; 37 within 24 hours and 9 within 1 hour of AMI presentation. People who used cannabis were more often men, cigarette smokers and obese. The statement adds that observational studies suggest cannabis may trigger AMI (refs 86, 87) and that the risk may be related to the timing of use.

key_findings.locator: Table 3, row Mittleman et al (p. e12); Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, paragraph (p. e17)
key_findings.note: Editors' observation from the statement's own numbers: the 4.8-fold estimate rests on few exposed people; the statement says 9 had smoked within 1 hour of AMI presentation (the timing used in the primary paper should be taken from Mittleman et al., 2001). Ref 37 (Frost et al., 2013) follows the same study, so the two rows are not independent. The primary paper is on this project's Tier B list.

key_findings.finding: Outcomes after MI, as relayed: long-term mortality 29% higher in people who used cannabis than in those who did not, not significant (95% CI 0.81–2.05; P = 0.28) (Frost et al., 2013, ref 37; 3886 MI survivors, National Death Index). In young adults with MI at two academic hospitals 2000–2016 (DeFilippis et al., 2018, ref 32; n = 2097), adjusted HRs of 1.99 for all-cause and 2.22 for cardiovascular mortality among people who used cocaine and marijuana (no intervals; whether the two exposures were combined is not said); the text says cannabis use was present in 6% of patients aged 50 or under with AMI. In hospital records from 8 states 1994–2013 (Johnson-Sasso et al., 2018, ref 40; more than 1.2 million AMI patients, 3854 or about 0.3% reporting cannabis use), the composite outcome (death, intra-aortic balloon pump, mechanical ventilation, cardiac arrest, shock) was not associated with cannabis use and mortality was lower (OR 0.79, no interval; short-term outcomes by the reference title); Desai et al., 2017 (ref 34) also report lower mortality in AMI patients who used cannabis. Smaller studies are said to show a signal toward higher mortality in coronary disease, although many of these findings were not statistically significant (refs 37, 87).
key_findings.page: pp. e11, e12, e17 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows DeFilippis et al, Desai et al (ref 34) and Frost et al (p. e11) and Johnson-Sasso et al (p. e12); Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, paragraph (p. e17)

key_findings.finding: AMI in health-record and inpatient databases, as relayed (exposure is recorded cannabis use or diagnosis codes; comparators are other patients in the same database; adjustment mostly not stated): Chami and Kim, 2019 (ref 31; Explorys 2011–2016; 292,770 people with a history of cannabis use, labelled the “cannabis abuse group”, against more than 10 million controls): 3-year cumulative AMI incidence 1.37% vs 0.54%, RR 2.53 (95% CI 2.45–2.61). Desai et al., 2019 (ref 33; National Inpatient Sample 2007–2014, more than 52 million hospitalisations, cannabis without other substance use): AMI admissions in young adults 0.23% vs 0.14%; arrhythmia and stroke more frequent, venous thromboembolism less frequent. Desai et al., 2017 (ref 34; 2010–2014): adjusted OR for AMI 1.079 (1.065–1.093); 35,771 of more than 2.4 million patients with AMI had a history of cannabis use. Patel et al., 2018 (ref 45; 2010–2014, 379,843 primary AMI admissions): 3.3% had a cannabis-use-disorder codiagnosis; AMI admissions among people who used cannabis rose 32% over 5 years (P = 0.001), mean age 41, with a 38% rise in women. Desai et al., 2018 (ref 35; 465,959 hospitalisations with recreational cannabis use): 1.2% for AMI, 1% for heart failure, 0.8% for arrhythmia, AMI rising from 1.4% to 1.8% over 2010–2014.
key_findings.page: pp. e11–e12 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows Chami and Kim and Desai et al (refs 33, 34, 35) (p. e11) and Patel et al (ref 45) (p. e12)
key_findings.note: Five of the inpatient analyses include the years 2010–2014 and four share a first author, so they are not independent replications. The ref 34 and ref 35 rows cannot be right as printed (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Heart failure, arrhythmia and stroke in inpatient data, as relayed: Kalla et al., 2018 (ref 41; National Inpatient Sample 2009–2010, more than 316,000 aged 18–55): in multivariable regression cannabis use predicted heart failure (OR 1.1) and stroke (OR 1.24), no intervals. Adegbala et al., 2018 (ref 27; about 4 million patients with heart failure): atrial fibrillation less frequent in people who used cannabis (19% vs 21%). Desai et al., 2018 (ref 36; 2010–2014): of 2,459,856 hospitalised people who used cannabis, 66,179 (2.7%) had arrhythmias, most often atrial fibrillation, rising from 2010 to 2014; in-hospital mortality in those with arrhythmia rose from 3.7% to 4.4%; no comparison group is reported. The text adds that case reports and observational studies support a temporal relationship with atrial fibrillation, though the evidence conflicts (refs 20, 22, 36).
key_findings.page: pp. e10, e11, e12 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 4th paragraph (p. e10); Table 3, rows Adegbala et al and Desai et al (ref 36) (p. e11) and Kalla et al (p. e12)

key_findings.finding: Stroke, as relayed: PATH Through Life (Hemachandra et al., 2016, ref 38; age cohorts 20–24, 40–44 and 60–64 years, surveyed 1999–2002): people with past-year cannabis use (n = 1043) had 3.3 times the rate of stroke or TIA (95% CI 1.8–6.3; P < 0.001), IRR 2.3 (1.1–4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco smoking; the excess was in people using weekly or more often (IRR 4.7, 2.1–10.7; adjustment not stated), with no elevation at lower frequency. BRFSS (Parekh et al., 2020, ref 68; adults aged 18–44): stroke adjusted OR 1.82 (1.08–3.10) for people who used marijuana against those who did not, 2.45 (1.31–4.60) for use on more than 10 days a month, 3.12 (1.40–6.97) for frequent use with combustible cigarettes and 2.63 (1.07–6.46) with e-cigarettes (adjustment set not stated). Against these, CARDIA found no association with stroke or TIA (ref 46).
key_findings.page: pp. e10, e12, e14, e17 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 5th paragraph (p. e10); Table 3, row Hemachandra et al (p. e12); Considerations in Special Populations › Young Adults, paragraph (p. e14); Patients With Cardiac Risk Factors, paragraph (p. e17)
key_findings.note: Cohort sizes differ between text (2404, 2530, 2551) and Table 3 (2383, 2525, 2547), and the text gives only the 3.3 before adjustment for stroke-related covariates (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Population trends around legalisation, as relayed: cardiac death rates rose 2.3% in men and 1.3% in women after medical cannabis laws (Abouk and Adams, 2018, ref 26; US vital statistics 1990–2014; design not described). Colorado (Wang et al., 2017, ref 49; more than 7 million hospitalisations and ED visits 2000–2015, plus poison-centre data): 0.3% of hospitalisations had cannabis-related billing codes, rising from 274 to 593 per 100,000 hospitalisations between 2000 and 2015; cannabis-related ED visits rose from 313 to 478 per 100,000 between 2011 and 2015; poison-centre calls rose after medical and recreational legalisation. French addictovigilance 2006–2010 (Jouanjus et al., 2014, ref 39): 35 of 1979 cannabis-related reports were cardiovascular, their share rising from 1.1% to 3.6%.
key_findings.page: pp. e10–e13 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 4th paragraph (p. e10); Table 3, rows Abouk and Adams (p. e11), Jouanjus et al (p. e12) and Wang et al (p. e13)
key_findings.note: The text says AMI hospitalisations and ED visits rose in states with legal cannabis (refs 26, 48), but none of these rows reports AMI-specific admissions (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Case-based and other studies, as relayed: a systematic review of published cases (Patel et al., ref 44; 62 patients with AMI and cannabis use): mean age 28, mostly men, AMI within 5 hours of last use, normal coronary angiograms in 37% and left anterior descending occlusion in 42% of angiograms. A systematic review of 85 studies, case reports and series (Richards et al., 2019, ref 47; 541,581 adults): 28 of 33 studies suggested higher risk of acute coronary syndrome and chronic cardiovascular disease; of 51 case reports or series with 62 people, 21 (34%) had cardiomyopathy and 14 deaths (23%) were attributed to acute coronary syndrome. HIV cohort (Lorenz et al., 2017, ref 42; 558 HIV-positive men, Multicenter AIDS Cohort Study 1990–2010): long-term heavy use independently associated with more cardiovascular events at ages 40–60 (no numbers). The text adds that AMI with cannabis occurs mostly in young men without ischaemic disease (refs 20, 22, 36).
key_findings.page: pp. e10, e12 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows Lorenz et al, Patel et al (ref 44) and Richards et al (p. e12); Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 4th paragraph (p. e10)
key_findings.note: Both reviews count 62 case patients; whether their case sets overlap cannot be checked from the statement. Table 3 dates ref 44 to 2019, the reference list to 2020.

key_findings.finding: Route (Monte et al., 2019, ref 19, as relayed in Table 3: one Colorado academic hospital 2012–2016, described as 9973 adult ED visits for cannabis use): people who had eaten cannabis more often had cardiovascular symptoms (8%) than people who had inhaled it (3%), and more often acute psychiatric symptoms and intoxication; inhaled cannabis was more often linked to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; cannabis-related visits rose 2012–2016. The text says eating cannabis “appears more likely” than smoking to cause adverse effects prompting acute care, particularly psychiatric and cardiovascular, citing Health Canada (ref 5) and attributing this to greater systemic absorption and a slower onset and peak.
key_findings.page: pp. e9, e12 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Acute Effects, 1st paragraph (starts p. e8; this passage on p. e9); Table 3, row Monte et al (p. e12)
key_findings.note: The library's card on the primary paper (sc_monte_2019) records 9,973 visits with a cannabis-related code, of which 2,567 were judged attributable to cannabis; the 8.0% vs 3.1% comparison is among 238 edible-attributed and 2,329 inhaled-attributed visits. Cite the primary card.

key_findings.finding: Acute effects and mechanisms, summarised from reviews (refs 5, 12, 13, 19 for acute effects; refs 20–22 for mechanisms and Figure 5): short-term use has been associated with tachycardia, premature ventricular contractions, atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmia, bronchitis, blurred vision, altered judgment, dysphoria and anxiety, paranoia and psychosis at higher doses, and impaired motor coordination. THC stimulates the sympathetic and inhibits the parasympathetic nervous system, increases heart rate, myocardial oxygen demand, supine blood pressure and platelet activation, and is associated with endothelial dysfunction and oxidative stress; CBD may lower heart rate and blood pressure. Figure 5 lists cardiomyopathy, MI, arrhythmias and sudden death, cerebral vascular accidents, and a questioned anti-atherogenic effect of CB2 activation.
key_findings.page: pp. e8–e9 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Acute Effects, 1st paragraph (starts p. e8); Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 1st paragraph (p. e9); Figure 5 (p. e9)
key_findings.note: Second-hand: refs 20–22 are reviews (DeFilippis et al., 2020; Pacher et al., 2018; Rezkalla and Kloner, 2019, co-authored by a writing-group member).

key_findings.finding: Smoke and carbon monoxide: compared with tobacco, smoking cannabis “regardless of THC content” is said to raise blood carboxyhaemoglobin 5-fold with 3-fold more tar (ref 23, Wu et al., 1988). Carbon monoxide intoxication is associated with endothelial dysfunction, lipoprotein oxidation, impaired oxygen binding and presentations from angina and AMI to cardiogenic shock and sudden death (ref 24, Kaya et al., 2016, a study of carbon monoxide poisoning).
key_findings.page: p. e9 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand. The clinical presentations come from carbon monoxide poisoning, not from cannabis smoking. NASEM 2017 (sc_nasem_2017) gives about four times the carbon monoxide and three to five times the tar for a 15-volunteer comparison; whether it is the same study cannot be checked here. Read Wu et al. (1988) before citing a multiple.

key_findings.finding: People with heart disease: in chronic stable angina, smoking one cannabis cigarette shortened exercise time to angina by 48% against placebo (ref 88, Aronow and Cassidy, 1974); in coronary disease with angina, cannabis use went with lower end-diastolic volume, stroke index and ejection fraction without change in end-systolic volume or cardiac index (ref 89, Prakash et al., 1975); sample sizes are not given. From NHANES 2005–2016, about 2 million (2.3%) of the 89.6 million US adults who reported marijuana use had cardiovascular disease (ref 20). The statement reasons that because cannabis raises myocardial oxygen demand and lowers supply, people with ischaemic disease could have more angina, particularly when it is smoked.
key_findings.page: p. e17 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Peripheral arteries: smoking cannabis has been associated, controversially, with a cannabis arteritis resembling thromboangiitis obliterans; more than 20% of lower-limb arteriopathy in young adults may be due to it, an estimate the statement says may be confounded because 97% of people who smoke cannabis also smoke tobacco (ref 50, Cottencin et al., 2010, a literature review; ref 51, a case report). It recommends considering cannabis arteritis in adults under 50 with peripheral vascular disease.
key_findings.page: p. e10 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cardiometabolic risk factors, as relayed: NHANES 2005–2012 (Alshaarawy et al., 2016, ref 28; 12,426 adults): cannabis use associated with higher systolic but not diastolic blood pressure, β = 1.6 (95% CI 0.6–2.7; units and adjustment not stated). Cross-sectional data link long-term continual use with metabolic syndrome (ref 91), while other studies report similar or lower rates of hyperglycaemia, raised fasting glucose and diabetes, and lower BMI, total and LDL cholesterol, in people who use cannabis (refs 92–98); Table 2 lists an observational association of long-term use with an improved metabolic profile.
key_findings.page: pp. e8, e11, e17 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table 2, row Metabolic syndrome, obesity, diabetes mellitus (p. e8); Table 3, row Alshaarawy et al (p. e11); Considerations in Special Populations › Patients With Cardiac Risk Factors, paragraph (p. e17)

key_findings.finding: Smoke and lungs, as summarised: cannabis smoke contains many of the carcinogens and mutagens of tobacco smoke (refs 5, 12, 20); limited and conflicting epidemiological evidence has not shown a robust and consistent association with cancers (ref 52, Ghasemiesfe et al., 2019, JAMA Network Open), with low-strength evidence for testicular cancer and mixed, confounded findings for lung cancer; the association of long-term heavy smoking without tobacco with COPD is unclear, though chronic bronchitis has been reported (refs 5, 12). For COVID-19 only tobacco figures are given (severe symptoms RR 1.4, 95% CI 0.98–2.00; ICU, ventilation or death RR 2.4, 1.43–4.04; ref 53); whether the risk extends to cannabis is said to be unknown.
key_findings.page: p. e10 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Smoking and Vaping Administration Concerns, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Ref 52 is the 2019 cancer review by Ghasemiesfe et al., not the 2018 respiratory review held as ghasemiesfe_2018.

key_findings.finding: Vaping and impurities: as of 18 February 2020, 2807 hospitalised patients with e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury and 68 confirmed deaths (29 states and DC) had been reported to CDC (ref 55, CDC web page); most patients reported THC-containing products; CDC linked THC products from informal sources to most cases without excluding nicotine products; vitamin E acetate was identified as a possible cause from a relatively small number of tissue samples (ref 56, Blount et al., 2019, MMWR). The statement nonetheless concludes that cannabis vaping should be avoided. It also cites an FDA warning (June 2018) about synthetic illicit cannabinoid products laced with brodifacoum (ref 54) and says unregulated over-the-counter topical CBD products may contain heavy metals, herbicides, pesticides and fungicides.
key_findings.page: pp. e10, e13 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Impurities, 1st paragraph (starts p. e10) and 2nd paragraph (p. e13)
key_findings.note: Ref 56 is the 2019 MMWR report, not the 2020 NEJM paper held as blount_2020. The brodifacoum source (ref 54) concerns synthetic cannabinoids, not cannabis.

key_findings.finding: Psychosis: the statement says significant preclinical, clinical and epidemiological evidence supports an association between cannabis, especially THC-predominant cannabis, and higher risk of psychosis and schizophrenia, particularly in people with a predisposition and those who start in early adolescence (refs 5, Health Canada, and 12, NASEM 2017; no primary study cited). From EU-GEI (ref 67, Di Forti et al., 2019; multicentre case-control): daily use against never use, adjusted OR 3.2 (95% CI 2.2–4.1) for psychotic disorder; daily use of high-potency cannabis (THC 10% or more) described as nearly 5 times the odds but printed as adjusted OR 3.2 (3.0–16.1) and described against low-potency cannabis (THC below 10%); the statement adds that the study did not account for genetic and environmental factors. It recommends that THC-predominant cannabis not be used by people with a personal history of psychiatric disorders (psychosis, schizophrenia, anxiety, mood disorders), a history of substance use problems, or a family history of schizophrenia.
key_findings.page: pp. e13, e14, e18 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Chronic Side Effects, paragraph (p. e13); Considerations in Special Populations › Young Adults, paragraph (p. e14); Patient Education and Considerations, paragraph (starts p. e17; this passage on p. e18)
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the high-potency figures cannot all be right (reporting issue) and no adjustment set is given. Cite Di Forti et al. (2019) from its own card.

key_findings.finding: Cognition and brain, from Health Canada, NASEM 2017 and Volkow et al., 2014 (refs 5, 12, 13; no primary study): early-onset use, typically before age 16–18, has been associated with reports of poorer sustained attention, lower overall or verbal IQ and worse executive functioning; neuroimaging studies suggest regular adolescent use “may lead to” altered cortical grey-matter development and reduced white-matter myelination. No effect sizes, comparison groups, tests or abstinence periods are given.
key_findings.page: p. e14 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Young Adults, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Depression and suicidality: a meta-analysis of 11 studies with 23,317 people assessed from adolescence to young adulthood (ref 66, Gobbi et al., 2019) found OR 1.37 (95% CI 1.16–1.62) for depression, 1.5 (1.11–2.03) for suicidal ideation and 3.46 (1.53–7.84) for suicide attempt in people who used cannabis against those who did not; the statement contrasts this with small observational reports of improved mood and anxiety in older adults. In US adults aged 50 or more (NESARC 2012–2013, ref 77), past-year cannabis use went with mental disorders in 33.2%, against 26.5% of people who had used cannabis only in the past and 19.4% of people who never had, possibly driven by self-medication (refs 78, 79).
key_findings.page: pp. e14, e16 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Young Adults, paragraph (p. e14); Geriatric Population, 1st paragraph (p. e16)

key_findings.finding: Dependence: the statement says “addiction” to cannabis has been reported in about 9% of people who use it, 17% of those who start in adolescence and 25% to 50% of those who use daily; this sentence carries no citation (the sentence before cites refs 57 and 58). From the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (ref 58, Hasin et al., 2016, whose title in the reference list names DSM-5 cannabis use disorder and NESARC-III, 2012–2013): 3 in 10 people who used cannabis in the past year met criteria for cannabis use disorder, a 30% prevalence the statement calls greater than that of alcohol use disorder (17.5%; denominator not stated). Named risk factors for use disorder: more edible use and vaping, higher THC and lower CBD content, younger age at first use (refs 59, 60). Prevalence may be underestimated, the statement says, because estimates rest on self-report and may use DSM-IV criteria without craving or withdrawal (ref 60). Tolerance develops with long-term use through reduced CB1 receptor availability (ref 20); withdrawal symptoms begin a few days after stopping or cutting down, peak at about 10 days and end after about 30 days (refs 5, 12).
key_findings.page: pp. e13, e21 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Chronic Side Effects, paragraph; Addiction Considerations, paragraph (starts p. e13); References, ref 58 (p. e21)
key_findings.note: Definitions differ: the uncited 9%, 17% and 25–50% figures have no stated definition or denominator; Hasin et al. counted DSM-5 use disorder among people who used in the past year; the DSM-IV caveat concerns other estimates (ref 60). Leung et al. (2020, sc_leung_2020) pools 22% for use disorder and 13% for dependence.

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: in a state with legalised medical and recreational cannabis (ref 70, Crume et al., 2018; the statement does not name the state), self-reported cannabis use during pregnancy was 5.7% ± 0.5% and early postnatal use among breastfeeding women 5.0% (95% CI 4.1–6.2); prenatal use was associated with low birth weight, OR 1.5 (1.1–2.1; P = 0.02), independent of maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use. A meta-analysis (ref 71, Gunn et al., 2016) found anaemia in pregnancy OR 1.36 (1.10–1.69) and infant low birth weight OR 1.77 (1.04–3.01), with a pooled mean difference in birth weight of 109.42 g (38.72–180.12; direction not stated). THC has been found in breast milk up to 6 days after the last recorded use (ref 69, US Surgeon General's 2019 advisory). The statement relays ACOG (2017) and AAP (2018) advice against use in pregnancy and discourages use while breastfeeding.
key_findings.page: pp. e14, e16 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Pregnant Women, 1st paragraph (p. e14) and 2nd paragraph (starts p. e14, continues p. e16)

key_findings.finding: Product strength and pharmacokinetics: newer commercial products are said to have a higher average THC content than products sold before 1996, 3.8% in the 1990s against 12.2% in 2014 (refs 13, Volkow et al., 2014, and 14, Klein, 2017, both secondary). Table 1 (no row-level sources; drawn from refs 5 and 7–11) gives for THC: inhaled onset seconds to minutes, bioavailability 2%–56%, duration 2–3 h; oral onset 30 min to 2 h, bioavailability 4%–20%, duration 5–8 h; half-life 20–30 h; protein binding 97%.
key_findings.page: pp. e3, e5 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Definitions and Cannabis Formulations, 3rd paragraph (p. e3); Table 1, THC row (p. e5)
key_findings.note: Second-hand; cite primary potency and pharmacokinetic sources on this project's lists instead. The DOSING section (pp. e4, e6, e8) is not extracted, by project rule.

key_findings.finding: Table 2 rows without row-level citations (footnote sources: Health Canada, NASEM 2017, Volkow et al., 2014, Segura et al., 2019, Wu et al., 2019): long-term (about 6–7 years) daily and weekly use has been associated with cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, possibly through CB1 downregulation and slower gastric emptying; human experimental data suggest a dose-dependent effect on sleep (shorter sleep-onset latency and more slow-wave and total sleep at low doses, disturbed sleep at high doses); in a nationally representative US sample, use at least once a month, but not less often, was associated with incident social anxiety disorder; in a retrospective propensity-matched analysis of 161,000 patients with heart failure, cannabis use went with lower in-hospital mortality (OR 0.197, 0.046–0.833), shorter stay (4.2 vs 4.8 days; P = 0.004) and lower costs (US$43,800 vs US$50,900; P = 0.039), data the table says have not been peer reviewed.
key_findings.page: pp. e7–e8 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows Nausea and vomiting and Anxiety and depression (p. e7) and Heart failure and Sleep (p. e8)
key_findings.note: The heart failure figures match the title of ref 18 (Wu et al., 2019, J Card Fail 25:S158, a meeting-abstract supplement).

key_findings.finding: Advice and policy: smoked or vaporised cannabis is generally not recommended, especially with asthma or COPD, and black- or grey-market products should be avoided; driving should be avoided because blood THC concentrations of 2–5 ng/mL are said to be associated with substantial driving impairment (ref 100, Hartman and Huestis, 2013, a review). Policy (Table 5 and closing section): remove cannabis from Schedule 1, standardise THC and CBD labelling and a unit of consumption, regulate CBD products, fund research, integrate cannabis into tobacco control and prevent use by minors; clinicians should be alert that cannabis or potent synthetic analogues might underlie severe cardiovascular events. Patient education (p. e18, no citation): people with long-term heavy use should be advised not to stop suddenly because of the risk of cannabis withdrawal syndrome, and to contact their provider if signs of withdrawal or hyperemesis syndrome arise.
key_findings.page: pp. e17–e19 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Patient Education and Considerations, paragraph (starts p. e17); Table 5 (p. e18); Policy Considerations and Future Directions, paragraph (starts p. e18)
key_findings.note: The driving threshold is second-hand; Hartman and Huestis (2013) is on this project's Tier B list. The advice on stopping is the AHA's recommendation without cited evidence; it is recorded here as such, not as a finding.

key_findings.finding: Transplantation: at least 7 US states forbid denying transplant listing for medical cannabis use (refs 83, a news article, and 84); in a web survey of heart-transplant providers in 26 countries (ref 84), 64.4% supported listing patients who use legal medical cannabis, 68.3% required a documented period of abstinence and 27.5% supported listing patients using legal recreational cannabis; inhaled cannabis may expose immunocompromised patients to pulmonary infections, most often aspergillosis (ref 85).
key_findings.page: p. e17 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Transplantation Patients, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Prevalence background: Figure 2, adapted from NSDUH 2018 (ref 1), shows 2016–2018 bars by substance, with a printed label of 43.5 million for marijuana in 2018 (read on the rendered page; the label is not in the text extraction); neither the figure nor its legend states the measure (for example past-year use) or the age base. The text says US use has risen particularly among people aged 18–25 and points to Figure 2, which has no age breakdown.
key_findings.page: pp. e1, e3 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 1st paragraph (p. e1); Figure 2 and legend (p. e3)

key_findings.finding: Hyperemesis: the statement says long-term, heavy (THC-predominant) use is associated with a higher risk of hyperemesis syndrome, with prodromal abdominal discomfort and nausea leading to intractable vomiting; the sentence carries no citation.
key_findings.page: p. e13 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Chronic Side Effects, paragraph (left column, continued in the right column below Table 3)
key_findings.note: Second-hand and uncited; Table 2 also lists the syndrome (see the key finding on Table 2 rows without row-level citations).

reporting_issues.issue: The two CARDIA citations in the text are swapped: the no-association finding for incident cardiovascular disease is cited to ref 29 (Auer et al., 2018, subclinical atherosclerosis) and the calcification finding in people who smoked tobacco to ref 46 (Reis et al., 2017, incident cardiovascular disease). Table 3 and the reference list attribute them the other way round.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e9–e12, e20–e21 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim traced through the text's citations would cite the wrong CARDIA paper; use the Table 3 attribution (Reis 2017 for incident disease, Auer 2018 for calcification) and read the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence that AMI hospitalisations and ED visits rose in states with legal cannabis cites refs 26 and 48. Ref 48 is Rodondi et al. (2006), a CARDIA analysis of diet and risk factors with no bearing on legalisation; ref 26 (Abouk and Adams) reports cardiac death rates; and the Colorado study (ref 49), probably intended, reports cannabis-related billing codes overall, not AMI.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e10–e13, e21 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: The AMI part of the sentence has no traceable support in the statement and should not be cited from it.

reporting_issues.issue: PATH Through Life (ref 38): the text gives cohort sizes of 2404, 2530 and 2551 and calls the study a retrospective evaluation; Table 3 gives 2383, 2525 and 2547 and calls it a population survey. The text reports only the 3.3-fold rate before adjustment for stroke-related covariates; Table 3 adds the adjusted IRR of 2.3 (1.1–4.5).
reporting_issues.page: pp. e10, e12 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the adjusted estimate and the sample sizes from the primary paper; the text alone overstates the association.

reporting_issues.issue: EU-GEI (ref 67): the text says daily use of high-potency cannabis gave nearly 5 times the odds of psychotic disorder but prints adjusted OR 3.2 (95% CI 3.0–16.1), the same 3.2 as the daily-use estimate before it and near the lower limit of its own interval; the comparator is given as low-potency cannabis, whereas the preceding estimate is against never use. Editors' calculation: the geometric midpoint of 3.0–16.1 is about 7.0, and that of the daily-use interval 2.2–4.1 about 3.0, so neither printed 3.2 is centred.
reporting_issues.page: p. e14 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one printed number is wrong; no EU-GEI figure should be cited from this statement (use Di Forti et al., 2019, Tier A).

reporting_issues.issue: Two Table 3 rows cannot be right as printed: Desai et al. 2017 (ref 34) is described as a sample of more than 2.4 million patients with AMI yet reports an adjusted OR for AMI with cannabis use (1.079), which cannot be estimated among people who all had AMI; Johnson-Sasso et al. (ref 40) report an incidence of AMI of 54% vs 20% in people under 50 who did and did not use cannabis within a sample of AMI patients, which reads as an age distribution rather than an incidence.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e11–e12 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: These rows misdescribe either the population or the measure; neither figure can be cited without the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Desai et al. 2018 (ref 35): 1.2% of hospitalisations of people with recreational cannabis use were for AMI overall, yet the annual AMI share is said to have risen from 1.4% to 1.8% over the same 2010–2014 period.
reporting_issues.page: p. e11 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: An overall share cannot lie below every annual share unless the two figures measure different things, which the row does not say; neither figure is usable as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: DeFilippis et al. 2018 (ref 32): Table 3 gives adjusted HRs of 1.99 (all-cause) and 2.22 (cardiovascular mortality) among people who used cocaine and marijuana, without intervals and without saying whether the exposures were combined, while the text (p. e17) attributes worse all-cause and cardiovascular mortality to cannabis use; the 6% prevalence in the text is not in the table.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e11, e17 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement cannot support a cannabis-specific mortality estimate after MI; read the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The text attributes the greater adverse-effect risk of edibles partly to increased systemic absorption compared with smoked cannabis, while Table 1 gives oral THC a bioavailability of 4%–20% against 2%–56% for inhalation.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e5, e9 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Internal inconsistency; claims about edibles should rest on the primary studies (Monte et al., 2019, has a card) and pharmacokinetic sources, not on this statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The dependence figures (about 9% of people who use cannabis, 17% of those who start in adolescence, 25–50% of those who use daily) carry no citation; the comparison of 30% cannabis use disorder among people who used in the past year (ref 58) with 17.5% alcohol use disorder gives no denominator for the alcohol figure; and a caveat about DSM-IV criteria without craving or withdrawal (ref 60) follows a study titled as DSM-5 (ref 58).
reporting_issues.page: pp. e13, e21 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: None of these figures can be cited from this statement as evidence; claims on how many people become dependent should use the primary sources with their definitions (for example Leung et al., 2020, which has a card).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 sorts claimed benefits into undefined categories and applies them inconsistently: under Known (conclusive or substantial evidence) it lists a harm (cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome after long-term daily or weekly use) and a finding of low efficacy (appetite and weight in HIV and cancer); under Inconclusive evidence (no RCTs) it lists rows citing small clinical trials (Huntington disease) and clinical studies (Parkinson disease); the heart failure row comes from data the table says are not peer reviewed, without a row citation. The footnote names Volko et al. for ref 13 (Volkow et al.).
reporting_issues.page: pp. e7–e8 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 2's categories are not grades and should not be quoted as the AHA's grading of evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: Misplaced citations: the Table 4 footnote names refs 62 (Weinberger et al., 2018) and 63 (Kristman-Valente et al., 2017), studies of cannabis and cigarette smoking, as sources for drug interactions, while the text cites refs 64 and 65 for the same content; ref 56 (Blount et al., 2019, a study of lung-lavage fluid in vaping lung injury) is cited for impurities in over-the-counter topical CBD products.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e13, e14, e16, e21 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation errors that limit tracing; check any interaction or impurity statement against its intended source.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction says US cannabis use has risen particularly among people aged 18 to 25 and points to Figure 2, which shows all ages by substance and year with no age breakdown and no stated measure or age base.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e1, e3 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: The age-specific statement has no support in the figure; prevalence claims should use NSDUH directly.

reporting_issues.issue: The pharmacology passages contain evident errors: the two cannabinoid receptors are called “2 CBD receptors” (p. e3), the receptors are said to affect the conversion of AMP to cAMP (p. e3), the Table 1 and Figure 5 footnotes expand CBD as cannabinoid, the interactions text names CYP “3A4/4” and “CP2D6” (p. e14), a THC content below 0.30% is called below the level of detectability while Figure 1 gives 0.3% as the legal definition of hemp (pp. e2–e3), and the risk named for severe liver disease is fibrosis or steatorrhea (p. e17), whereas Table 2 speaks of steatosis (p. e8). The editors also note, from general pharmacology rather than this source, that THCA is usually described as decarboxylated by heating, not in the liver as stated on p. e2.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e2–e3, e5–e6, e8–e9, e14, e17 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not cite this statement for pharmacology or pharmacokinetics; use primary pharmacokinetic sources (for example Huestis, 2007, and Grotenhermen, 2003, on this project's lists).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 describes Monte et al. (ref 19) as 9973 adult ED visits for cannabis use; the library's card on the primary paper (sc_monte_2019) records 9,973 visits with a cannabis-related code, of which 2,567 were judged attributable to cannabis, and the 8% vs 3% comparison of cardiovascular symptoms is among attributable visits only.
reporting_issues.page: p. e12 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Cross-source discrepancy: the statement's denominator overstates the attributable visits about fourfold; cite the primary card.

reporting_issues.issue: Two CARDIA rows give different ever-use figures without definitions (84% reported a history of cannabis use in Reis et al., ref 46; 38% reported ever using in Rodondi et al., ref 48); smaller citation slips include Table 3 dating Patel et al. (ref 44) to 2019 while the reference list gives 2020, ref 60 printed as 2019 with volume 77 (this project's list dates the same DOI to 2020), and the CARDIA acronym expanded without Artery in the text and Table 3 footnote, unlike the reference titles.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e9, e12–e13, e21 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not cite a CARDIA prevalence of cannabis use from this statement; match references by DOI.
